proposals.relationship: Hartman identifies Du Bois’s formal experimentation as an inspiration for the project that became Wayward Lives.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Creative Independent interview, originally 18 April 2018 and redisplayed 3 February 2021, answer on teaching Du Bois, explicitly praises the formal variety of The Souls of Black Folk and says his ideas shaped her current project. That project is still described as forthcoming Wayward Lives in this witness. She also retains a critical relation to masculine intellectual self-fashioning and the Philadelphia survey’s pathologizing categories. This positive debt complements, without replacing, edge_1286; neither original Du Bois book nor the complete Hartman monograph is newly read.
primary_locators: 2018 interview, answer to Du Bois at 150 question; subsequent Philadelphia Negro answer

proposals.relationship: Hartman explicitly credits Foucault with shaping her understanding of power and discourse while finding limits in his account of domination.
proposals.evidence_note: Own BOMB 2022 answer to the agency/domination question expressly acknowledges the thinker’s importance to her concepts of knowledge, power and genealogy. Her Venus in Two Acts (2008), 2–3/notes 4–6, 5/note 18 and 10/note 33, also uses Lives of Infamous Men and Archaeology of Knowledge to frame archival visibility and violence. This is a qualified intellectual debt, alongside her separately stated criticism; it is not wholesale adherence or a new reading of Foucault’s originals. Interviewer Jackson’s formulations are distinguished from Hartman’s own acknowledgment.
primary_locators: BOMB 2022, Hartman answer beginning Yes, the question of agency

proposals.relationship: Hartman argues that Foucault’s treatment of extreme domination does not adequately explain racial slavery and enslaved practice.
proposals.evidence_note: Own BOMB 2022 agency answer identifies reading The Ethic of Care alongside The Subject and Power as a turning point: she found no precise account of the domination she needed to analyze, and distinguished enslaved social death from the constrained freedom of a wife. She retains tremendous respect for his thought and says this limit required her to develop an account of her own. This is her retrospective, specific criticism rather than a new independent adjudication of the originals. Her chronology expressly places Scenes before Mbembe’s Necropolitics; no anachronistic claim that the latter caused the 1997 book.
primary_locators: BOMB 2022, complete Hartman agency answer from Yes, the question of agency through the distinction between wife and enslaved

proposals.relationship: Hartman uses de Certeau’s account of historical writing to think about making a place for the living and questioning historical knowledge.
proposals.evidence_note: Own Venus in Two Acts, 14 and note 42, explicitly identifies these two historiographical operations and then reads Octavia Butler’s Kindred as a model for practice along those lines. The note cites The Writing of History in a 1992 manifestation. This resource neither promises recovery of lost lives nor removes Hartman’s insistence on failure and narrative restraint. Butler’s distinct role is retained; neither cited book is newly read, and the citation date is not asserted as first publication.
primary_locators: Venus 2008:14/n42, with Butler/n43 and concluding limits

proposals.relationship: Hartman invokes Scott’s histories of peasant anarchism as a comparative resource for thinking about African and diasporic radical struggle.
proposals.evidence_note: Own White Review 2020 answer about readers reaching the end of Lose Your Mother explicitly names the political scientist James Scott’s work on South Asian peasants before asking about African resistance to predatory state formations and its diasporic imagination. This is her bounded comparative use, not an assertion that Scott originated African radicalism, a proven personal encounter or a demonstrated cause of her 2007 book. No particular unread Scott title is guessed. Her larger account also credits African writers and other Black traditions that remain explicit missing-endpoint holds.
primary_locators: White Review June2020, answer beginning At a certain moment, second paragraph on James Scott
